Rudolf Steiner — Who Was He?

Rudolf Steiner was born in 1861 in Kraljevec, in what is now Croatia, and grew up in rural Austria. From an early age he possessed an unusually developed inner life — an experience of the spiritual world as real and living, alongside an equally rigorous scientific intellect. He completed a doctorate in philosophy in Vienna, edited Goethe's scientific writings, and wrote his foundational philosophical works — including The Philosophy of Freedom (1894) — before turning his full attention to the practical task of changing the world.

Steiner was not primarily a theorist. He was a builder — of schools, of a new medicine, of a new agriculture, of new arts. He lectured over 6,000 times in his lifetime, gave birth to Waldorf education, biodynamic farming, anthroposophic medicine, eurythmy, speech formation, social threefolding and a renewal of the arts. He died in 1925, having founded a movement that would outlast him by a century and spread to every corner of the earth.

His life's work rested on one conviction: that the human being is a being of body, soul and spirit — and that every dimension of our civilisation, from how we grow food to how we educate children to how we heal the sick, must be rebuilt on that recognition.

The Birth of Waldorf Education

On 7 September 1919 — in the ruins of post-war Germany, just one year after the end of the First World War — Rudolf Steiner opened the first Waldorf school in Stuttgart. It was founded at the request of Emil Molt, the director of the Waldorf-Astoria cigarette factory, for the children of his workers. It was radical from the first day: no distinction between rich and poor, boys and girls taught together, art woven through every lesson, teachers with real freedom to teach.

Steiner gave the teachers a simple but profound instruction: know the child. Not the curriculum, not the examination, not the standard — the child. The whole child. The child who is thinking and feeling and willing. The child who is growing not just in body but in soul.

Over one hundred years later, there are more than 1,100 Waldorf schools in over 60 countries — making it the largest independent school movement in the world. From Auckland to Nairobi, from São Paulo to Seoul, from tiny home classrooms to beautiful school campuses, the work that began in Stuttgart continues.

The Heart of Waldorf Education
☀️ Head — Thinking
Education of the mind — not with dry facts alone, but through imagination, story, wonder and inquiry. The child's thinking is kindled, not stuffed. Knowledge earned through experience stays forever.
💛 Heart — Feeling
Education of the feeling life — through music, painting, drama, storytelling, the arts and the beauty of the natural world. A child whose feeling life is nourished grows into an adult with empathy, reverence and moral courage.
🙌 Hands — Willing
Education of the will — through handwork, woodwork, gardening, cooking, building and making. A child who has worked with their hands knows their own capacity. They have courage, patience and the quiet confidence of one who has made something real.

These three — thinking, feeling and willing — are not three separate subjects. They are three dimensions of every human being, and every lesson in a Waldorf school tends to all three at once. A mathematics lesson is not only about numbers — it is sung, drawn, moved, told as a story. A painting lesson is not only about colour — it cultivates patience, attention and the quiet satisfaction of beauty made by one's own hands. This is not efficiency. It is education in the deepest sense: the drawing out of what was always there.

What Makes Waldorf Different

In a Waldorf school, the same teacher stays with a class from Grade 1 through Grade 8. Not because it is convenient, but because the relationship between teacher and child is itself the curriculum. The teacher who knows a child across eight years knows their soul. That knowledge is irreplaceable.

Reading and writing are not formally introduced until age 6–7 — when the child's developmental readiness naturally calls for it. Before that, the child lives in story, in song, in movement, in the warmth of imitative play. There are no screens. No standardised tests in the early years. No comparison, no ranking, no rush. Instead: rhythm, beauty, reverence for the world and deep respect for the unhurried process of growing up.

The Waldorf year breathes with the seasons — Michaelmas, Martinmas, Advent, Christmas, Candlemas, Easter, Pentecost, St. John's. The festivals are not decorations. They are a living calendar, connecting the child to the rhythms of the earth and the deeper meaning woven through the year. Every season has its colour, its grain, its quality of light.

This Directory — For You
Whether you are a parent discovering Waldorf for the first time, a teacher of many years looking for a particular resource, a homeschooling family building your rhythm from scratch, or a practitioner seeking connection with the wider community — The Waldorf Path is for you.

This directory has been gathered with love and care: 38 sections, 500+ resources, worldwide. Teachers, mentors, books, instruments, wool suppliers, felt artists, biodynamic farms, anthroposophic doctors, psychology resources, German publishers, Spanish books, seasonal guides, songs, verses and so much more — all in one place, organised around the three pillars of Waldorf living.

May it serve your path.

  • ⭐ Suzanne Down — Juniper Tree School of Story & Puppetry Arts 🇺🇸USA (Boulder, Colorado). The foremost Waldorf puppetry educator in the world. Juniper Tree School of Story and Puppetry Arts was founded over 40 years ago and has now trained 30+ groups of professional puppeteers. Suzanne's journey began at Emerson College in England where she studied hand puppetry with the legendary Gisela Bittleston. She went on to found Juniper Tree Puppets, a marionette theatre performing fairy tales and folk tales from around the world with multicultural marionettes, cultural costume and music accompaniment. She taught puppetry in a Waldorf school in British Columbia, ran children's marionette troupes for Grades 4–6, and then began training other teachers internationally — traveling to early childhood conferences, libraries and schools as a trainer for decades before bringing all training online. Rudolf Steiner said that a young child who does puppet shows will not have the modern adolescent issues of pessimism, sarcasm and depression — Suzanne has dedicated her life's work to making this gift accessible to every parent and teacher.

  • Puppetry in the Waldorf Curriculum — Why It MattersPuppetry is a core feature of Waldorf early childhood education. In kindergartens, the teacher tells stories through simple table or lap puppets — the child watches with open eyes and mouth, absorbing image and gesture without rational interference. Puppetry nourishes imagination, language, moral sense and the soul forces of the young child. The different puppet types are used at specific developmental stages: lap/table puppets for the very young (0–6), rod puppets for early grades, marionettes for Grades 4–6, hand puppets from Grade 2 onward.—

🗣️ Creative Speech & Speech Formation — Specialists Worldwide
What is Creative Speech / Speech Formation? Creative Speech (Sprachgestaltung) is an art form initiated by Rudolf and Marie Steiner — the artistic forming of human speech. In Waldorf schools it is a curriculum subject from Grade 1 through Grade 12. Every main lesson begins with speech — verses, poems, drama. The teacher's voice has a profound effect on children. "The sounds themselves are our teachers — they will be the best teachers we will ever have." — Rudolf Steiner.

🧠 Anthroposophic Psychology — Worldwide
What is Anthroposophic Psychology? Anthroposophic Psychology approaches counselling and psychotherapy with the understanding that the human being is composed of body, soul and spirit. The psychologist and patient work toward developing a deeper understanding of the nature and potential of each human life. Through studying an individual's biography — exploring accomplishments, challenges and life patterns — an awareness becomes possible of the steps needed for a healthier movement into the future.

"Psyche" is Greek for soul. Soul is the workshop, employing the capacities of thinking, feeling and willing — head, heart and hands — wherein the individuality (the "I") meets the challenges of a life. Based on the work of Rudolf Steiner, further developed by Bernard Lievegoed, Karl König, Robert Sardello, Dennis Klocek, James Dyson, William Bento, Georg Kühlewind and others.

🏛️ Organisations & Training

Programmes: 3-year Certificate Programme (open to counsellors, teachers, therapists, priests, farmers, artists, healers and anyone with questions about the human soul) · 3-year Internship Programme for graduates · 2-year Professional Certification in Anthroposophic Psychotherapy (for licensed clinicians) · Free webinar series 2024–2025. Member of AHA and IFAPA. Recognised by the Medical Section at the Goetheanum. Founded by William Bento PhD. anthroposophicpsychology.organthroposophicpsychology.org

Via anthroposophicpsychology.orgVia Goetheanum · anthroposophicpsychology.org

📕 Must-Read Books — Your Essential Reading Guide For parents · For teachers · For homeschoolers · Steiner's own education texts · By stage ▾
📕 This is your reading guide — a curated list of the most essential Waldorf books, organised by who you are: parent, teacher or homeschooler. It answers: where do I start, what do I read next?

📚 Looking for books organised by your child's age and developmental stage? See the next section: Books & Publications — By Developmental Stage.

The single most recommended first book across every Waldorf school reading list worldwide: You Are Your Child's First Teacher by Rahima Baldwin Dancy. If you read nothing else, read that.
🌱 For Parents — If You Are New to Waldorf (Start Here)
  • ⭐ 1. You Are Your Child's First Teacher — Rahima Baldwin DancyHawthorn Press / Ten Speed Press. The single most recommended first book for Waldorf parents worldwide. The first book in America to popularise Rudolf Steiner's insights regarding the developmental needs of young children. Covers birth to age 6: language and cognitive development, appropriate toys, nourishing artistic abilities, discipline, early childhood programmes, toilet training and using home life as curriculum. Today's society pressures us into overstimulating young children — Dancy speaks up for a rational approach that helps children be children. "If you are just going to get one book as an introduction to Waldorf parenting — this is the one." Revised edition with updated resources. Rating: 4.01/5 from 1,837 readers on Goodreads. Hawthorn Press / Ten Speed Press / Celestial Arts.Hawthorn Press · Amazon · florisbooks.co.uk
  • ⭐ 2. Beyond the Rainbow Bridge — Barbara J. Patterson & Pamela BradleyMichaelmas Press. The ideal companion to You Are Your Child's First Teacher. A wonderful starting place for understanding the Waldorf approach to the early years — gentle parenting through rhythm, simple toys, less haste and respectful presence. Patterson draws on years of parent-child class groups with honest questions from parents and practical suggestions. Covers birth through age seven. Explains the "rainbow bridge" — the passage from the spiritual world into earthly life — with warmth and clarity. Rating: 4.01/5 from 679 readers. Michaelmas Press.Michaelmas Press · Amazon · waldorfpublications.org
  • ⭐ 3. Simplicity Parenting — Kim John Payne MEdBallantine Books. The most widely read Waldorf-adjacent parenting book of the last 20 years — and not just in Waldorf circles. Using the extraordinary power of less to raise calmer, happier and more secure kids. Simplifying the home environment, filtering media, protecting rhythm and simplifying the schedule. Based on Payne's work with thousands of families. Not explicitly Waldorf but shares all the same values. Rating: 4.22/5 from 16,000+ readers. A book that genuinely changes family life. Ballantine Books / Vermilion (UK).Ballantine Books · Amazon · good bookshops everywhere
  • ⭐ 4. Heaven on Earth: A Handbook for Parents of Young Children — Sharifa OppenheimerSteinerBooks. The most practical Waldorf home handbook. How to develop a family rhythm, how to celebrate festivals at home, how to create a beautiful, ordered home environment for children. Grounded, warm and deeply applicable. Covers daily, weekly and seasonal rhythms, the Waldorf approach to play, story, art and nature. Rating: 4.34/5 from 686 readers — exceptionally highly rated. SteinerBooks / Anthroposophic Press.SteinerBooks · steinerbooks.org
  • 5. Free to Learn — Lynne OldfieldHawthorn Press. A clear, warm guide to the principles and methods of Waldorf early childhood education — drawing on kindergarten experience from around the world. Stories, helpful insights, observations and photographs. Explains what lies behind the Waldorf kindergarten — imitation, reverence, rhythm, play, the artistic environment — without being academic. An excellent bridge between the philosophical and the practical. Hawthorn Press.Hawthorn Press · florisbooks.co.uk
  • 6. Understanding Waldorf Education: Teaching from the Inside Out — Jack PetrashGryphon House. The most accessible overview of the whole Waldorf curriculum for parents who want to understand what happens in every grade. Clear, non-jargon writing. Goes inside the Waldorf classroom — main lesson books, seasonal festivals, the arts, developmental stages. Highly recommended for parents of school-age children wanting to understand what their child is doing and why. Rating: 3.75/5 from 651 readers. Gryphon House.Gryphon House · Amazon
🌿 For Parents — Going Deeper
  • ⭐ School as a Journey: The Eight-Year Odyssey of a Waldorf Teacher and His Class — Torin FinserSteinerBooks. The most beloved book about life inside a Waldorf school. Told in Finser's lively, humorous style — one class teacher's journey with his class from Grade 1 through Grade 8. Parents considering Waldorf find enormous comfort here: the dedication, creativity and warmth of Waldorf teaching made vivid and human. Illustrates the remarkable relationship between teacher, student, family and school community across eight years. Rating: widely loved. Essential reading for any Waldorf parent. SteinerBooks / Anthroposophic Press.SteinerBooks · steinerbooks.org
  • ⭐ Waldorf Education: A Family Guide — Pamela Fenner & Karen Rivers, eds.Michaelmas Press. A comprehensive practical guide for parents — covering child development, the Waldorf curriculum from kindergarten through high school, special needs, festivals, home life and how to find and choose a Waldorf school. One of the most complete family reference guides. Michaelmas Press.Michaelmas Press · waldorfpublications.org
  • Seven Times the Sun: Guiding Your Child Through the Rhythms of the Day — Shea DarianGilead Press. The book about daily rhythm. Morning, midday, afternoon, mealtime, bedtime — each moment of the day treated as a sacred opportunity. Songs, verses, stories and practical suggestions for each transition. Deeply Waldorf in spirit without using the name. Beautiful, lyrical writing. One of the most-loved books on Waldorf family rhythm. Gilead Press.Gilead Press · Amazon
  • All Year Round — Druitt, Fynes-Clinton & RowlingHawthorn Press. The complete seasonal and festival companion for Waldorf families. Songs, verses, poems, crafts and activities for every season and festival throughout the year. Autumn, Harvest, Michaelmas, Martinmas, Advent, Christmas, Candlemas, Easter, Midsummer. A permanent fixture on Waldorf family bookshelves. Rating: 4.24/5 from 240 readers. Hawthorn Press.Hawthorn Press · florisbooks.co.uk
  • Between Form and Freedom — Betty StaleyHawthorn Press. The essential guide to the teenage years in Waldorf education. A practical, compassionate and insightful guide for parents and teachers of adolescents — covering the developmental tasks of the high school years, social life, sexuality, identity and the relationship between parents and teenagers. Betty Staley is one of the most respected voices in Waldorf high school education. Hawthorn Press.Hawthorn Press · Amazon
  • Working with Anxious, Nervous and Depressed Children — Henning KöhlerSteinerBooks. Essential reading for parents and teachers of children who struggle. Henning Köhler's deeply compassionate and practically useful guide to understanding and supporting children with anxiety, nervousness and depression — from an anthroposophical perspective. Available in English and Spanish (Editorial Rudolf Steiner). One of the most cited child psychology books in Waldorf education. SteinerBooks.SteinerBooks · steinerbooks.org
🎓 For Teachers — The Essential Shelf
  • ⭐ The Education of the Child (GA 34) — Rudolf SteinerSteinerBooks / Anthroposophic Press. The foundational short essay — read this first of all Steiner's education texts. Three developmental stages, the relationship between education and soul-spiritual development, the principles of the Waldorf curriculum. Short (under 50 pages), accessible, profound. Available free at rsarchive.org. Every Waldorf teacher and parent should have read this.rsarchive.org (free) · SteinerBooks
  • ⭐ The Foundations of Human Experience (Study of Man) (GA 293) — Rudolf SteinerSteinerBooks. The deepest and most demanding education text. Fourteen foundational lectures given to the first Waldorf teachers in Stuttgart, August–September 1919 — before the school opened. The most complete account of child development, the threefold human being and the psychology of education. Not easy — but of inexhaustible depth. Read slowly, repeatedly, in a study group. SteinerBooks / Anthroposophic Press. Also free at rsarchive.org.rsarchive.org (free) · SteinerBooks
  • ⭐ The Kingdom of Childhood (GA 311) — Rudolf SteinerSteinerBooks. Seven lectures given in Torquay, England, August 1924 — Steiner's last series of education lectures before his death. Covers child development, the incarnation process, the child as sense organ, imitation, fantasy and the kindergarten, as well as teaching main lessons and numbers. More accessible than Study of Man. An ideal second Steiner education text. SteinerBooks / Rudolf Steiner Press.rsarchive.org (free) · SteinerBooks
  • ⭐ Waldorf Education: Ideas of Rudolf Steiner in Practice — Christopher Clouder & Martyn RawsonFloris Books. The most comprehensive modern overview of the complete Waldorf curriculum K–12 by two of the most respected British Waldorf educators. Covers every subject area, the developmental stages, the school as a social organism, teacher development and assessment. Essential reading for any teacher entering the Waldorf profession. Floris Books 🇬🇧florisbooks.co.uk
  • ⭐ Waldorf Education: A Human Approach (Education Towards Freedom) — Frans CarlgrenFloris Books / Rudolf Steiner Schools Fellowship. A survey of Waldorf schools worldwide with hundreds of photographs. One of the most visually rich introductions to Waldorf education — showing real school life across many countries and grades. A book that has introduced more teachers to Waldorf than almost any other. Floris Books.florisbooks.co.uk
  • Phases of Childhood — Bernard LievegoedFloris Books. The essential developmental guide for Waldorf teachers. Belgian psychiatrist and anthroposophist Bernard Lievegoed describes the three major developmental phases of childhood in exquisite detail — the dreaming phase (0–7), the imaginative phase (7–14) and the thinking phase (14–21) — and their implications for education. One of the most widely read books in Waldorf teacher education worldwide. Floris Books.florisbooks.co.uk
  • Lighting Fires: Deepening Education Through Meditation — Jørgen SmitHawthorn Press. On the Waldorf teacher's inner development — meditation, self-knowledge, the relationship between the teacher's inner life and the quality of their teaching. The most important book on teacher self-development in the Waldorf tradition. Hawthorn Press.Hawthorn Press · florisbooks.co.uk
  • Child Health Guide — Michaela Glöckler & Wolfgang GoebelFloris Books. The standard medical reference for Waldorf families and school doctors. Comprehensive guide to child health from an anthroposophic medical perspective — child development, common illnesses and their meaning, fever, vaccinations, anthroposophic remedies. Dr Glöckler was head of the Medical Section at the Goetheanum for many years. Floris Books.florisbooks.co.uk
🏡 For Waldorf Homeschoolers
  • ⭐ Teaching Waldorf: A Curriculum for Grades 1 through 8 — VariousAWSNA / Waldorf Publications. The most complete grade-by-grade Waldorf curriculum guide available for homeschoolers and teachers. waldorfpublications.orgwaldorfpublications.org
  • ⭐ Wonder, Reverence, Respect: For the Very Young — Johanna Voors, ed.WECAN. Compiled articles on the development of the young child, the Waldorf approach to the first three years, imitation and the body, rhythm and the environment. Essential reading for parents and carers of very young children in a Waldorf context. WECAN Books.waldorfearlychildhood.org
  • Waldorf Homeschool Handbook — Donna SimmonsChristopherus Waldorf Curriculum. Practical guidance for homeschooling families using a Waldorf approach. Donna Simmons has been guiding homeschool families for over 20 years. christopherus.comchristopherus.com
  • In a Nutshell: Meditations for Parents and Teachers — Marjorie SpockSteinerBooks. Short, profound meditations on education and child development for daily contemplation. A beloved companion for Waldorf parents and teachers. SteinerBooks.SteinerBooks
  • The Genius of Play — Sally JenkinsonHawthorn Press. The definitive book on Waldorf play. Celebrates the spirit of childhood play — free, unstructured, imaginative play — and makes the case for protecting it in a world that increasingly undervalues it. Essential reading for any parent or early childhood educator. Hawthorn Press.Hawthorn Press · florisbooks.co.uk
🌀 The Philosophical Foundation — Steiner's Core Spiritual-Scientific Works
Why these books matter for Waldorf families and teachers: Waldorf education is not a set of methods — it is the practical expression of a complete spiritual-scientific understanding of the human being. The books below are the roots of the entire tree. You do not need to read them before understanding or practising Waldorf — many people live happily with Waldorf for years before encountering them. But when you are ready, they will transform your understanding of everything. "These are not books to be read once and set aside. They are books to be lived with for years."
  • ⭐ The Philosophy of Freedom / Intuitive Thinking as a Spiritual Path (GA 4) — Rudolf SteinerRudolf Steiner, 1894. The philosophical cornerstone of everything Steiner ever said or did. Steiner's clearest and most demanding statement of epistemology, moral autonomy and the method of intuitive thinking. Argues that true human freedom lies not in the absence of external constraint but in the capacity to act from pure thinking — from love for the deed itself, with no other motive. The book that establishes Steiner's credentials as a serious philosopher before anthroposophy properly begins.

    "What I want to present in this book is a science of freedom. To resolve all other questions and riddles is not the primary task of philosophy — that task is to establish the foundations of all other knowledge."

    Why Waldorf teachers should read it: Every element of Waldorf pedagogy — the freedom to teach from living understanding rather than fixed methods, the respect for each child's individuality, the refusal to indoctrinate — flows from this book's philosophical foundation. The Waldorf teacher who has truly understood the Philosophy of Freedom teaches from freedom. The teacher who has not yet read it may still teach beautifully — but will not understand why.

    Recommended translation: Michael Wilson (Rudolf Steiner Press) is widely preferred. Also: "Intuitive Thinking as a Spiritual Path" (Anthroposophic Press, trans. Michael Lipson) — same text, excellent translation. Available free at rsarchive.org.    rsarchive.org (free) · Rudolf Steiner Press · SteinerBooks
  • ⭐ Theosophy: An Introduction to the Spiritual Processes in Human Life and in the Cosmos (GA 9) — Rudolf SteinerRudolf Steiner, 1904. The most accessible entry point into Steiner's complete worldview. Introduces the fourfold human being — physical body, life body (etheric), soul body (astral) and ego — as well as the soul members and spirit members. Covers reincarnation, karma and the soul's journey between death and rebirth. Short (under 200 pages), clear and beautifully structured. Despite the potentially off-putting title — "Theosophy" — this is not Blavatsky's Theosophy but Steiner's own spiritual science, using the same vocabulary in his own way.

    Why Waldorf teachers and parents should read it: The threefold human being underpins all of Waldorf education — the three-seven year developmental stages, the relationship between thinking, feeling and willing, the education of head, heart and hands. Theosophy is where you learn what the threefold human being actually is in Steiner's own words. Rating: 4.12/5 from 791 readers on Goodreads. Available free at rsarchive.org.    rsarchive.org (free) · SteinerBooks · Rudolf Steiner Press
  • ⭐ How to Know Higher Worlds / Knowledge of the Higher Worlds (GA 10) — Rudolf SteinerRudolf Steiner, 1904. Steiner's fundamental handbook for inner development. A precise, practical manual of exercises and stages for developing spiritual perception — with careful attention to psychological safety, grounding and balance. More than 100 years after first publication, it remains — alongside meditation, channelling, remote viewing and astral projection — uniquely precise in its instructions for inner training, protective exercises and grounding.

    Why Waldorf teachers should read it: Steiner insisted that the Waldorf teacher's inner development — their capacity for genuine reverence, wonder and self-knowledge — is at least as important as their pedagogical skill. This book is the guide to that inner work. Rating: 4.21/5 from 1,947 readers. The most widely read Steiner book worldwide. Available free at rsarchive.org.    rsarchive.org (free) · Rudolf Steiner Press · SteinerBooks
  • ⭐ An Outline of Esoteric Science (Occult Science — An Outline) (GA 13) — Rudolf SteinerRudolf Steiner, 1910. Of all Steiner's books, this one perhaps comes closest to containing the whole of his spiritual teaching in one volume. Systematic presentation of the constitution of the human being, the evolution of the earth and humanity through the great cosmic stages (Saturn, Sun, Moon, Earth, Jupiter, Venus, Vulcan), reincarnation and karma in depth, and the complete path of initiation. Dense, demanding — and inexhaustibly deep.

    "Given his energetic involvement in practical initiatives and extensive lecturing, Steiner had very little time to write books. Of those he did write, four titles form an indispensable introduction to his later teaching: Knowledge of the Higher Worlds, Occult Science, The Philosophy of Freedom and Theosophy."

    Read slowly. Read with a study group if possible. Do not expect to understand it on first reading — each re-reading over years reveals new dimensions. Available free at rsarchive.org. SteinerBooks edition recommended. Rating: 4.23/5.    rsarchive.org (free) · SteinerBooks · Rudolf Steiner Press
  • The Foundation Stone Meditation — Rudolf Steiner (Christmas Conference 1923)The spiritual cornerstone of the re-founded Anthroposophical Society — given by Steiner at the Christmas Conference in Dornach, December 1923. A meditation verse in four movements, one for each season, encompassing the whole of anthroposophy in concentrated poetic form. Often described as the most complete spiritual verse Steiner ever gave. Read slowly, meditatively, alongside a commentary — many good ones available (Sergei Prokofieff, Florin Lowndes). Available free at rsarchive.org and in print via SteinerBooks and Rudolf Steiner Press.rsarchive.org (free) · SteinerBooks
  • Christianity as a Mystical Fact (GA 8) — Rudolf SteinerRudolf Steiner, 1902. Steiner's exploration of the Christ event as the central mystery of human evolution — seen not through faith but through spiritual-scientific investigation. Bridges ancient mystery traditions (Greek, Egyptian, Persian) and the significance of the Resurrection for human consciousness and the future of the earth. "The turning point of time." A book of great depth and beauty. Available free at rsarchive.org. Rudolf Steiner Press / SteinerBooks.rsarchive.org (free) · SteinerBooks
Reading order recommended by the Rudolf Steiner Archive: Begin with Theosophy and Knowledge of Higher Worlds. Then An Outline of Esoteric Science and The Philosophy of Freedom. Then Christianity as a Mystical Fact. Then explore the lecture cycles (GA 95–125 are good starting points). All available free at rsarchive.org.
📜 Rudolf Steiner's Own Education Texts — A Reading Path
Start withThenThenFor depth
The Education of the Child (GA 34) — short, accessible, essential. Free at rsarchive.org The Kingdom of Childhood (GA 311) — 7 lectures, Torquay 1924. Warm and practical. The Foundations of Human Experience / Study of Man (GA 293) — the deepest text. Read in a study group. Rhythms of Learning (GA selections) · The Child's Changing Consciousness (GA 306) · Soul Economy (GA 303)
All of Steiner's education lectures are available free in English at rsarchive.org. The GA numbers are the definitive reference system for his collected works (Gesamtausgabe). Note: translations vary in quality — SteinerBooks / Anthroposophic Press editions are generally recommended over older translations.

SteinerBooks

WECAN

SteinerBooks

WECAN
🌱 STAGE 1 — BIRTH TO AGE 3 · Physical Development Dominant · Learning Through Imitation

The child is building the physical body. Walking, speaking and thinking emerge as the three great achievements. The child is one with the world and learns entirely through imitation. Every impression goes all the way in. Warmth, rhythm, nourishment and sensory richness are the medicine.

🫀 The Child from Birth to Three in Waldorf Education
Patzlaff, Grah-Wittich & Howard (eds). WECAN. Physical, emotional and spiritual development in the first three years. Concrete suggestions for home and care settings.
WECAN
🫀 The First Three Years of the Child
Karl König. SteinerBooks. Walking, speaking, thinking — the three great developmental achievements. Written by the founder of Camphill. Deep, beautiful, essential.
SteinerBooks
🫀 Raising Sound Sleepers
Dr. Adam Blanning MD. SteinerBooks (2024). Helping infants and young children develop healthy sleep through sensory awareness and rhythm. Anthroposophic family medicine.
SteinerBooks 2024
🫀 A Waldorf Guide to Children's Health
Dr. Michaela Glöckler, Dr. Wolfgang Goebel & Dr. Karin Michael. Floris. Essential family health reference from birth through adolescence. Illnesses, symptoms, anthroposophic treatments. The Waldorf family's household medical book.
Floris Books
💛 The Dignity of the Young Child
Dr. Michaela Glöckler. WECAN. Care for the first three years. The inner life and dignity of the infant and what babies truly need from adults.
WECAN
💛 The Creative Word
Daniel Udo de Haes. WECAN. The young child's experience of language and storytelling. How speech forms the soul of the very young child in the first years.
WECAN
☀️ Creative Play for Your Baby
Christopher Clouder & Janni Nicol. Hawthorn. Open-ended, age-appropriate play from birth. Natural toys, sensory play, Waldorf-informed developmental activities for 0–2 years.
Hawthorn Press
☀️ Nurturing Children and Families
Sarah Baldwin. WECAN. One model of a parent-child programme in a Waldorf school. Songs, movement, seasonal crafts and rhythm for babies and toddlers.
WECAN
🌸 STAGE 2 — AGES 3–7 · Kindergarten Years · Play, Imagination & Imitation

The life forces begin to free from the physical body. The child learns through imitation, imagination, movement and doing. No formal academic instruction yet. Free creative play is the most important "work." Fairy tales, seasonal rhythms, handwork, domestic activity, outdoor play, songs and verses are the curriculum.

🌻 STAGE 3 — AGES 7–12 · The Grade School Years · Learning Through Feeling & Imagination

The life forces are freed from physical growth and now build memory, temperament, habit and conscience. Children learn through feeling and imagination under a beloved class teacher. Fairy tales, fables, myths, history through stories, handwork, music and movement balance academic content. The 9-year change (ages 9–10): the child suddenly feels separate from parents and peers — a profoundly vulnerable moment needing gentle, wise support.

🫀 Physical — Body, Handwork, Health, Movement

A Waldorf Guide to Children's Health (continued)
Glöckler, Goebel & Michael. Floris. Childhood illnesses, fevers, ear infections, common complaints throughout the school years. Why fever has developmental value. The household medical reference.
Floris Books

Michael Martin (ed) (UK). How handwork — knitting, weaving, carving, sewing — builds will forces, fine motor coordination and physical intelligence in the school-age child, Grades 1–8.
SWSF Publications

Audrey McAllen (UK). Hawthorn. Movement-based remedial programme for reading, writing or arithmetic difficulties. Specific movement sequences that support brain integration. Grades 1–6.
Hawthorn Press

🔥 STAGE 4 — AGES 12–14 · Pre-Adolescent Transition · Lower Middle School

The astral body begins its birth. Puberty approaches. Children begin to think critically and form their own opinions. Abstract thinking emerges. They need ideals and heroes. The curriculum reflects the renaissance of humanity — perspective drawing, electricity, chemistry, biography. Tremendous physical and emotional upheaval begins.

🫀 Making Math Meaningful: Grades 6–8
Jamie York (USA). Business math, irrational numbers, square roots, basic algebra, geometry — paced to the emerging capacity for abstract thinking in the pre-adolescent years.
Jamie York Press

Ballantine

Rawson, Avison & Richter. Floris. Roman history, physics, chemistry, perspective drawing, world geography, algebra, biography — how each subject meets the 12–14 year old developmentally.
Floris Books
🌟 STAGE 5 — AGES 14–21 · High School · Adolescence · Ego Development & Independent Thinking

The ego (I) begins its birth. Independent thinking, idealism and abstract judgment emerge. The curriculum becomes rigorous — sciences, world literature, philosophy, history, mathematics, arts. The teacher becomes a guide. The great questions of life begin to be wrestled with honestly.

🫀 A Waldorf Guide to Children's Health (adolescent chapters)
Glöckler, Goebel & Michael. Floris. Puberty, sleep, substance use, mental health — through an anthroposophic medical lens. Continues to be relevant through age 18.
Floris Books

Hawthorn Press
💛 Education for Adolescents
Rudolf Steiner. SteinerBooks. The foundational text on the adolescent stage — how the ego forces work, what the young person needs from education. Used in Sunbridge and CfA high school programs.
SteinerBooks

🧥 Clothing & Dress-Up Costumes Natural fabrics · Dress-up · Retailers ▾
Waldorf clothing philosophy: Natural fibres only — wool, silk, cotton. No synthetic materials next to the skin. Temperature-regulating fibres support the child's developing warmth organism. Dress-up uses open-ended natural silks and simple capes rather than character costumes.

🎻 Music & Instruments Makers · Retailers · Education ▾
"The human being is a musical being, and the making of music is essential in experiencing what it is to be fully human." — Rudolf Steiner.

In Waldorf education, music is not a separate subject — it is woven through every moment of the day. The child who grows up in a musical home — where songs are sung, where instruments are played, where rhythm marks each transition — arrives at school already deeply nourished. Whether or not your child attends a Waldorf school, you can bring the living world of Waldorf music into your home.
🧒 Music for Children — What Children Play & When
Age / GradeWhat the Child ExperiencesInstruments
Birth–Age 3
Parent & Child		 The parent sings — the child listens and absorbs. Simple lullabies in the Mood of the Fifth. No percussion, no stimulating rhythms. Just the human voice, floating and open. The parent's voice is the first and most important instrument the child encounters. The parent's singing voice · Kinder lyre played by parent · Gentle bells
Ages 3–7
Kindergarten		 Pentatonic songs sung together in circle time. The teacher sings — the children join when ready, never forced. Seasonal songs, nature verses, transition songs. The teacher plays the kinder lyre or pentatonic lyre to accompany singing and settle the room. Children may ring small bells or tap simple percussion. Kinder lyre (teacher) · Pentatonic glockenspiel · Small bells · Boomwhackers (some schools)
Grade 1 / Age 7 The child receives their own Choroi pentatonic flute and begins to play. Pentatonic songs connected to fairy tale images and letter introduction. Lyre introduced in many schools. All music through imitation — no notation yet. Improvisational games and listening cultivated. The experience of music remains entirely in the feeling life. Choroi pentatonic flute (their own) · Pentatonic lyre · Chime bars
Grade 2 / Age 8 Pentatonic flute and lyre continue. Exploration of contrasts — high and low, loud and soft, fast and slow. Pentatonic songs about nature, seasons, saints and fable characters. Call and response develops listening. Pentatonic songs with a definite tonic ending introduced. First experience of simple ensemble playing. Choroi pentatonic flute · Pentatonic lyre · Glockenspiel
Grade 3 / Age 9 The 9-year change — the child moves to the diatonic flute (recorder) and diatonic music. Rounds and canons introduced. String instruments begin — most Waldorf schools begin individual string lessons (violin, cello) in Grade 3. Music notation taught formally. Diatonic songs with a clear tonic and ending. Sopranino / soprano recorder · Violin or cello (begins) · Diatonic glockenspiel
Grades 4–5 / Ages 10–11 Recorder continues. Individual string instrument lessons deepen. Rounds, canons, two-part singing begins. Orchestral instruments may be introduced. Music theory begins — scales, intervals, modes, notation. The child can now hold their part in an ensemble. Class orchestra forms. Recorder (C soprano) · Violin / cello / viola · Class orchestra
Grades 6–8 / Ages 12–14 Full choral and orchestral work. Part singing, harmony, music theory deepened. Instruments: full recorder range (soprano, alto, tenor), orchestral strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion may be added. Music history connected to history curriculum. Class choir. School concerts. Alto/tenor recorder · Orchestral instruments · Class choir · Class orchestra
High School / Ages 14+ Choral society, chamber music, world music, folk traditions of cultures studied, composition, music theory deepened. Musical theatre and school play often feature live music. Students may choose orchestra, choir, recorder ensemble or individual study. Individual instrument · School orchestra · Choir · Composition
🏡 Bringing Waldorf Music Into the Home
Start with the kinder lyre
The kinder lyre (also called kinder harp or pentatonic lyre) is the most versatile Waldorf home instrument. It is tuned to the pentatonic scale so everything played on it sounds beautiful — parents don't need to know music to begin. Play it softly at bedtime, during rest time, or to accompany singing. Children aged 2+ can pluck it. The most recommended first instrument for a Waldorf home. Available from Choroi, Auris, Harps of Lorien and many Waldorf suppliers.
Ages 0+ · All families
Sing every day — without apology
The most important thing you can do musically for your child is simply sing — even if you think your voice is imperfect. Children do not hear imperfection. They hear love, presence and warmth. Sing the transition songs in this directory. Sing the seasonal songs. Sing the meal blessing. Sing a lullaby. The voice you have is perfect enough.
All ages · All families
The pentatonic flute (Ages 6+)
A Choroi pentatonic flute is the first instrument a Grade 1 Waldorf child receives. It is tuned to the pentatonic scale — only five notes, all harmonious. Children learn to play by imitation, not notation. At home, the parent learns alongside the child. Simple seasonal songs, lullabies and nature melodies can be played within the first few lessons. Available from Choroi.org · Waldorf instrument suppliers · approximately €25–35.
Ages 6+ · Grade 1
Pentatonic glockenspiel (Ages 3+)
The Auris pentatonic glockenspiel is a beloved home instrument — six or eight bars tuned to the pentatonic scale, in a beautiful wooden frame. Played with a soft mallet. A child can play it alone without producing discord — every note combination sounds harmonious. Ideal for toddler musical exploration and early childhood free play. Available from Auris (aurisinstruments.com) · Bella Luna Toys · Waldorf suppliers worldwide.
Ages 2+ · Kindergarten
Recorder (Ages 9+ / Grade 3)
The soprano recorder is the standard Grade 3–8 Waldorf school instrument — affordable, portable, beautiful when well played. Mollenhauer and Moeck are the preferred German wooden recorder makers used in Waldorf schools. Avoid plastic recorders where possible — the wooden tone is warmer and more alive. A good wooden soprano recorder costs approximately €20–40. Lessons at home: the Waldorf recorder songbook series by many publishers.
Ages 9+ · Grade 3
String instruments (Ages 9+ / Grade 3)
Most Waldorf schools begin violin or cello in Grade 3. Hiring rather than buying is strongly recommended for the first 1–2 years. Waldorf string education follows a strongly aural, imitative approach — the Suzuki method is compatible and widely used alongside Waldorf pedagogy. Practice 10–15 minutes daily in the early years is far more valuable than occasional long sessions.
Ages 9+ · Grade 3
Singing games and circle time at home
The simplest and most complete music practice for young children is the singing game — movement, song, rhythm and social interaction all in one. Books: Singing Games for Families, Schools and Communities (Anna Rainville & Laurie Clark, WECAN); Dancing As We Sing (Nancy Foster, WECAN); Let Us Form a Ring (Nancy Foster, WECAN). These three books contain everything a family needs to bring Waldorf music to life at home.
Ages 2–10 · Home circle
Harps of Lorien — Kinder Lyres (USA)
Raphael Weisman has been making kinder lyres for over 20 years. The most trusted North American maker of pentatonic children's lyres — used in partnership with the Christopherus Waldorf homeschool curriculum. High quality, affordable, made with care. harpsoflorien.com
harpsoflorien.com

🌍 Skin Tone Crayons & Pencils — Celebrating Every Child
Why skin tone art supplies matter in Waldorf education: Every child should be able to draw themselves, their family and their friends in their own true colours. Traditional "flesh" crayons represented only one skin tone. A growing range of beautiful skin tone crayon and pencil sets now offer the full spectrum of human skin — from the palest to the deepest. In Waldorf main lesson books and art projects from Grade 1 onward, children draw and paint people. Having the right colours is an act of dignity and inclusion.

🏠 Waldorf Boarding Schools — Worldwide
What is a Waldorf boarding school? A small number of Waldorf and Steiner schools around the world offer residential boarding — students live on or near the school campus during term time, immersed in the full Waldorf rhythm of work, art, nature and community life. Waldorf boarding schools are rare and precious — they offer a particularly deep experience of Waldorf education, where the daily and weekly rhythms extend beyond classroom hours into the fabric of daily living.

Note: The Waldorf World List (waldorf-international.org) is the most comprehensive and up-to-date directory of all Waldorf and Steiner schools worldwide. Always verify boarding availability directly with the school as arrangements change.
SchoolCountryNotesWebsite
⭐ High Mowing School 🇺🇸 Wilton, New Hampshire, USA Founded 1942 by Beulah Hepburn Emmet. The only Waldorf boarding school in the USA and the oldest Waldorf high school in North America. Day and boarding, co-educational, Grades 9–12. Rural campus in the Monadnock Region. 300 students. Green and white colours. highmowing.org
⭐ Michael Hall Waldorf School 🇬🇧 Forest Row, East Sussex, England Founded 1925. The oldest Steiner school in Britain. Set in Kidbrooke Park on the edge of Ashdown Forest. Ages 3–18. 400+ students. Boarding available for upper school students. The historical heart of British Waldorf education. michaelhall.co.uk

🤲 Finger Games & Gesture Plays What they are · Why they matter · Wilma Ellersiek · Books · Trainers · Free resources ▾
What are finger games? Finger games (also called finger plays, hand gesture games or gesture plays) are short rhythmic verses or songs accompanied by specific hand and finger movements. They are one of the most ancient and universal forms of early childhood activity — found in every human culture worldwide.

In Waldorf early childhood education, finger games are not entertainment or time-filling — they are a precise developmental tool. Rudolf Steiner observed that "nimbleness in finger movement will translate in later life to nimbleness in thinking." Every finger game a young child learns is building the neurological foundations for reading, writing, mathematics and social connection.

Wilma Ellersiek (1921–2007) — teacher of music, speech and dance at the Stuttgart State Academy for Music and Performing Arts — devoted the later part of her life to researching the specific effects of rhythm, movement and language on the young child. The gesture games she developed became foundational to Waldorf early childhood programmes worldwide. Her five books, published by WECAN, are the gold standard.
🌱 Why Finger Games Matter — The Developmental Case
🖐 Fine motor development
Strength and coordination in the small muscles of the hands and fingers directly prepares for writing, instrument playing and all handwork. Fingers that can gesture, tap, weave and point with precision are fingers ready to hold a pencil, knit a stitch or bow a violin string.
Ages 2–9
🧠 Bilateral brain coordination
Most finger games use both hands together — or alternate left and right in sequence — crossing the body's midline. This bilateral coordination connects the brain's two hemispheres and is the same neurological foundation required for reading and writing. Finger games are, in the most literal sense, brain-building.
Ages 0–7 · Brain
📖 Language and memory
Verse, rhyme, repetition and movement together are the most powerful tools for language acquisition available to the young child. The physical gesture anchors the word in the body — the child who acts out "the spider climbs up the drainpipe" remembers the word "drainpipe" forever. Memory is embodied.
All ages · Language
🎵 Rhythm and musicality
Coordinating speech with movement develops internal rhythm — the foundation of musicality, mathematics and social synchrony. A child who can keep a steady beat with their fingers while saying a verse is a child whose nervous system is learning to organise time.
Ages 2–8 · Music
🔢 Number sense
Counting games and one-to-one correspondence are naturally embedded in finger games — "one little finger, two little fingers..." Long before formal arithmetic, the child's fingers teach them that numbers are real, embodied and reliable.
Ages 3–7 · Maths
💛 Loving connection
The most important dimension of finger games for the very young child is the intimate human contact — an adult fully present, playing, touching, singing. The hand games in Ellersiek's Giving Love, Bringing Joy are specifically designed as touch games for parent and baby. This loving presence is itself nourishment.
Birth–Age 5 · Relationship
✨ How to Teach a Finger Game
The adult does the game first — completely, beautifully, with presence and joy. The child watches. Then the adult does it again. Children join in when they are ready — never asked to perform or show you. The verse is repeated daily, often for weeks, before the child has it fully. The repetition is not boring — it is the point. Each repetition deepens the physical memory and the language.

Sing or speak with warmth, not exaggerated cheerfulness. The gesture should be natural and loving, not mechanical or theatrical. Speak clearly and let the rhythm carry you. The child's own body will follow when it is ready.

🕊️ Verses in Waldorf Education Morning · Blessing · Transition · Seasonal · Daily free resource ▾
What is a Waldorf verse? A verse in the Waldorf tradition is a short poem, recitation or blessing used at a specific moment in the day — to open the morning, bless the meal, begin handwork, mark a transition, or close the afternoon. Verses are distinct from songs (which have melody) and from the Calendar of the Soul (which is a weekly meditation). They are spoken aloud — often by the whole group together — with care, rhythm and presence. A verse makes the ordinary sacred.

Verses are not inherently religious. They are poetic invocations of the living world — of the earth, the sun, the seasons, the food on the table. Many have been passed from teacher to teacher for generations and their original authors are often unknown or unrecorded. They belong to the living tradition of Waldorf education.
🌅 Today's Daily Verse — Free Resource
Loading today's verse…

The verse rotates daily through the seasonal and daily verse collection. Speak it slowly, morning and evening.

☀️ Traditional Waldorf Verses — Opening & Closing

These verses are used in Waldorf schools worldwide. They are not religious texts — they are poetic invocations of the living world. Many have been passed from teacher to teacher for generations; their original authors are often unknown or unrecorded.

🌅 Good Morning — Kindergarten Opening (Traditional)
Good morning, dear Earth
Good morning, dear Sun
Good morning, dear trees
And the flowers, everyone
Good morning, dear bees
And birds in the trees
Good morning to you
And good morning to me
Kindergarten · Opening
☀️ The Sun with Loving Light — Rudolf Steiner (Grades 1–4)
The Sun with loving light
Makes bright for me each day
The soul with spirit power
Gives strength unto my limbs
In sunlight shining clear
I revere, oh God
The strength of humankind
Which thou so graciously
Hast planted in my soul
That I with all my might
May love to work and learn
Grades 1–4 · Rudolf Steiner
🌍 The Earth Is Firm (Traditional)
The earth is firm beneath my feet
The sun shines bright above
And here I stand, so straight and strong
All things to know and love
Grades 1–3 · Morning
🌙 Parent-Child Opening Verse (Traditional)
Down is the earth, up is the sky
Here is my family and here am I
The golden sun is shining
Up in the sky so blue
Good morning, happy morning
Good morning, sun, to you
Parent & Child · Ages 0–3
🍽 Meal Blessing (Traditional)
The earth that grows for us this food
The sun that makes it ripe and good
Dear Earth, dear Sun, by you we live
Our loving thanks to you we give
All Ages · Meal Time
📖 Story Time Song (Traditional)
Fairies of the story time
Come and share your stories with me
I am listening with my ears
And I'm sitting quietly
Kindergarten–Grade 2 · Transition
🌅 Morning Has Come (Traditional)
Morning has come
Night is away
Rise with the sun
And welcome the day
All Ages · Morning
🕯️ Lantern Song — Martinmas (Traditional)
I go with my little lantern
My lantern goes with me
Above the stars are shining
Below us shines the street
Laterne, Laterne
Sonne, Mond und Sterne
Martinmas · November
🌊 Transition Songs — For the Rhythmic Waldorf Day

It is a much more joyful experience to sing "This is the way we wash our hands" rather than shouting "Come and wash your hands now!" while your toddler cheekily runs around the house with muddy hands. Keep your transition songs simple enough for children to sing by themselves — you will hear children singing the songs on their own, reminding themselves of the steps to accomplish a job. The best transition songs: short (4–8 lines), rhythmic, action-based and sung to a simple melody the child can join in with immediately.

🧼 Wash, Wash, Wash Your Hands (Traditional Waldorf)
Wash, wash, wash your hands
Make them nice and clean
Wash the germs right down the drain
Make them nice and clean
Sung to the tune of Row, Row, Row Your Boat. Simple, rhythmic, action-based. Children naturally mime the washing motion. Used in Waldorf kindergartens and homes worldwide before meals and after outdoor play.
Ages 2+ · Before meals · After play
🧼 This Is the Way We Wash Our Hands (Traditional)
This is the way we wash our hands
Wash our hands, wash our hands
This is the way we wash our hands
Before we eat our food
Sung to the tune of Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush. Add verses: "This is the way we dry our hands… / This is the way we comb our hair…" — endlessly adaptable for any routine.
Ages 2–6 · Daily routines
🧹 Clean-Up Song — Twinkle Version (Traditional Waldorf)
Twinkle, twinkle little star
Stop and clean up where you are
It's time to put the toys away
We will play another day
Twinkle, twinkle little star
Stop and clean up where you are
Sung to the tune of Twinkle Twinkle Little Star. Gets the job done and offers encouragement of fun the next time the children are together. Warm, reassuring — "we will play another day" honours the child's play rather than simply ending it.
Ages 2–7 · Tidy-up time
🧹 Everybody Clean Up (Traditional)
Everybody clean up, clean up, clean up
Everybody clean up, after lunch
Trash in the trashcan, recycle in the bin
When we work together we all win!
Light, energetic and community-minded — "when we work together we all win" is deeply Waldorf in spirit. Change words to suit context: "clean up after play / clean up before we go."
Ages 3–8 · After meals · Tidy-up
🎒 Getting Ready to Go Outside (Traditional Waldorf)
Put on your snow boots — tug, tug
Put on your winter coat — zip, zip
Put on your cosy hat — whoop!
Put on your mittens now — both hands!
We're playing in the snow, hurray!
Sung to The Farmer in the Dell or another simple tune. The onomatopoeic words (tug, zip, whoop) delight young children and prompt the action simultaneously. Adaptable for any season — "put on your sun hat / put on your raincoat."
Ages 2–6 · Getting dressed · Seasonal
🚶 Walking Down the Hall (Traditional)
We're walking down the hall
We're walking down the hall
Let's keep together, friends
We're walking down the hall
A simple moving verse for transitions between rooms or from indoors to outdoors. The rhythm of the song naturally regulates the pace of children's feet. Change to "We're walking to the garden / We're walking to the table."
Ages 2–7 · Moving transitions
👋 Welcome Song — Each Child Named (Traditional)
We're all here today
We're all here today!
Clap, clap, oh clap your hands
We're all here today!
[Child's name] is here today
Clap, clap, oh clap your hands
[Child's name] is here today!
A favourite for opening circle because clapping keeps everyone involved. Children are invited to dance in the circle after their verse. Every child is named, seen and celebrated. A profound act of recognition for the young child.
Ages 2–7 · Morning circle · Opening
🛏️ Rest Time Verse (Traditional)
The flowers, they grow on your ten little toes
All the way up to your little nose
The petals unfold as you rest and be still
Breathe in the perfume and be, if you will
A therapeutic touch verse for rest time — gentle massage of toes while singing. Can be accompanied by light touch to help the child settle. Particularly beautiful after outdoor play before the midday meal.
Ages 1–5 · Rest time · Therapeutic touch
🍞 Before Baking / Cooking (Traditional Waldorf)
Little hands so busy
Kneading, kneading, kneading
Round and round the dough goes
Warm and soft and growing
Into the oven, into the oven
Warm and golden baking
A simple verse to sing while kneading bread dough — one of the classic Waldorf kindergarten activities. The words follow the action. Children love joining in with the kneading motion.
Ages 3–7 · Baking · Handwork
🌙 Goodbye / End of Day (Traditional Waldorf)
Now we take our love and light
Back to mother smiling bright
Back to father, kind and warm
Holding baby in their arms
Goodbye now, goodbye!
Blessings on our day!
The classic parent-child closing verse. Bridges the child from the group back to the family with warmth and care. The day is not simply "over" — it is consciously returned to the home with a blessing.
All Ages · Closing · Goodbye
💡 How to Create Your Own Transition Songs
Choose a familiar tune — Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush, The Farmer in the Dell, Row Row Row Your Boat, are all good choices. Then make up a rhyme — one concept per verse. You will usually need 8 beats to fit into the song — play around with it until your song is satisfying! The best transition songs are personal, specific and sung consistently — the same song, the same tune, every single day. That is what makes them work. Children begin to self-regulate simply upon hearing the opening notes.
Tip for parents & teachers

🎶 Songs in Waldorf Education Why music matters · Pentatonic · Seasonal · By grade · Songbooks ▾
Why songs and verses are at the heart of Waldorf education: "The human being is a musical being, and the making of music is essential in experiencing what it is to be fully human." — Rudolf Steiner. In Waldorf schools, every single day begins with song. Songs are not a separate subject — they are woven into every transition, every meal, every season, every grade curriculum. A song to light the candle. A song to begin handwork. A song to bless the snack. A song to welcome autumn. A song to say goodbye. Music is the connective tissue of the Waldorf day.

Songs are woven through every Waldorf day and every Waldorf grade. See also the companion Verses section in this directory for morning verses, meal blessings, transition verses and the Calendar of the Soul.
🌟 Why Pentatonic Music for Young Children?
The pentatonic scale is a five-note musical scale — D, E, G, A, B — that removes two notes from the familiar seven-note scale. Rudolf Steiner recommended pentatonic music for young children due to its ethereal and dreamy quality. Steiner believed that young children, who are still closely connected to the spiritual world, benefit from staying in a dreamy, imaginative state.

The pentatonic scale "brings awareness of man within the divine world order" as Steiner said in his lectures. While the diatonic scale is a grounding experience and an inner look at man, the pentatonic scale is an "expansion into the vast universe" — it is constantly expanding, never ending, like the little improvised songs a child makes up naturally.

When does this change? The pentatonic scale is used from birth through approximately Grade 2. At the stage when children crave the diatonic scale — the traditional scale (CDEFGAB) with its clear rhythms and beats and songs with a clear beginning and end — teachers introduce it. This typically coincides with the 9-year change (Grade 3), when the child incarnates more fully into the physical world. The transition from pentatonic to diatonic mirrors the child's own transition from dreaming to waking consciousness.
The Mood of the Fifth
Before the pure pentatonic scale, Steiner identified an even earlier musical mood — the "mood of the fifth" — for the very youngest children (ages 0–5). This is an open, floating, unresolved musical quality using the interval of a fifth. It creates a sense of infinite space, like a question hanging in the air without needing an answer. Waldorf lullabies and nursery songs in this mood have a quality of hovering between earth and heaven — perfect for the baby and toddler still arriving into the world. Julius Knierim's Quintenlieder (Mood of the Fifth songs) is the classic resource.
Birth–Age 5
Pure Pentatonic
From approximately ages 3–7 (Kindergarten through Grade 2), the pentatonic scale is used exclusively. Songs feel open, dreamy, never quite resolved. There are no leading tones pulling toward a final note — the child floats in the music as they float in play. Instruments tuned to the pentatonic scale — kinder harp, pentatonic lyre, glockenspiel — create a harmonious and ethereal sound perfectly suited to young children.
Ages 3–7 · K–Grade 2
Diatonic Scale & Folk Songs
Many folk songs are either in the pentatonic scale or in one of the traditional modes — these tonalities are precursors to our more familiar major and minor scales and lend themselves well to improvisation. From Grade 3 onward, the full diatonic scale arrives with the 9-year change. Music now has a clear tonic, a clear ending. The child stands on firm ground musically as they do developmentally.
Grade 3+ · Age 9+
Why no minor key for young children?
Young children should not be given songs in minor keys — the sadness, heaviness and earthward pull of minor tonality is too much for the soul of a child still arriving into the world. Minor keys appear in the Waldorf curriculum from Grade 3–4 onward, once the child has established themselves on the earth. Before this, all songs are major-inflected or pentatonic.
Important principle
🌿 How Songs Are Used Throughout the Waldorf Day
MomentType of Song/VerseWhy
Morning circle / warm-upOpening verse + seasonal songs + movementCircle time is a special gathering each morning when you sing songs together, recite verses, use movement and do fingerplays — pulled together into a seasonal or story-based theme. It wakes up the body, the feeling life and the will simultaneously.
Transitions between activitiesShort transition songs (4–8 lines)Teachers are taught to sing little songs to indicate a transition in activities — these songs ignite the child and connect with them on an emotional level. Far more effective than instructions or bells.
Lighting the candleCandle lighting verseThere are little songs for blessing candles before they are lit and normally songs again to blow them out. Every sacred moment is marked with music.
Meal blessing / snack timeGratitude verse sung togetherConnects the child to the earth, sun and living world that provided the food. Cultivates reverence and gratitude before eating.
Handwork & craftActivity songs sung while workingThere are little songs to introduce handwork and baking activities. Singing while working connects will and feeling — the hands work more rhythmically and the soul is at peace.
StorytellingStory songs, character songsThere are little songs incorporated into stories. A character who sings a verse every time they appear deepens the child's imaginative engagement.
Outdoor play / nature walksSeasonal nature versesSongs about the seasons, animals and natural world deepen the child's observation and connection. A song about froggies in winter makes frog awareness a living reality.
Closing circle / goodbyeClosing verse or songBrings the day to a conscious, rhythmic close. The child leaves held by beauty rather than simply dismissed.
Festivals & seasonsFestival-specific songsMichaelmas songs, Advent songs, Easter songs, Midsummer songs — each festival is sung into life weeks before it arrives. The anticipation lives in the body through song.
Main lesson warm-up (Grades 1–8)Grade-appropriate verse + recorder + singingIn the early grades, circle becomes not only a music and movement gathering, but a time to practice math in an active way, work on drama and speech exercises, and practice the recorder.
📋 Songs & Music by Waldorf Grade — What Children Sing & Play
Grade / AgeScale / KeyInstrumentsSong Types
Parent & Child · Ages 0–3Mood of the Fifth · LullabiesVoice · Pentatonic lyreLullabies, nursery rhymes, finger songs, gentle nature verses. No dramatic content. Floating, open, unhurried.
Kindergarten · Ages 3–6PentatonicKinder harp · Glockenspiel · VoiceSeasonal nature songs, circle songs, finger games (Ellersiek), transition songs, meal blessings, gnome and fairy songs. Teacher sings; children gradually join.
Grade 1 · Age 7PentatonicPentatonic flute (Choroi) · LyreFirst Graders are given wooden pentatonic flutes and begin to play themselves. Songs connected to fairy tale images and letter introduction. Singing games. Morning verse.
Grade 2 · Age 8Pentatonic (moving toward diatonic)Choroi flute · LyrePentatonic songs with a definite tonic ending. Songs about nature, seasons, saints and fable characters. Exploration of contrasts — loud and soft, high and low, fast and slow — still in the realm of feeling.
Grade 3 · Age 9Diatonic begins · Major & minor introducedRecorder (C) · VoiceOld Testament songs, farming songs, shelter songs. The 9-year change is met musically — songs now have a clear beginning and end, mirroring the child's new sense of standing on firm ground.
Grade 4 · Age 10Diatonic · ModesRecorder · Orchestral instruments beginNorse mythology songs, rounds and canons, first experience of harmony. Traditional folk songs in modal scales. Solo singing begins.
Grade 5 · Age 11Full diatonic · Modal explorationRecorder · Orchestral · Pentatonic lyreTraditional American folk songs such as "The Erie Canal" for American geography. Scales, modes, Circle of Fifths. Songs sung in two or three parts — children develop skill in harmony.
Grades 6–8 · Ages 12–14Full diatonic · Major & minor · HarmonyClass orchestra · Individual instrumentPart singing, choral work, music theory introduction, composition exercises. Songs matched to history curriculum — medieval, Renaissance, folk traditions of the civilisations studied.
High School · Ages 14+Full musical rangeIndividual instrument · Choir · EnsembleChoral society, chamber music, folk music from world cultures, composition. Music theory deepened. The school play typically includes original or arranged music.
🍂 Seasonal Songs — A Year in Song
🌱 Spring Songs
Spring is announced through song weeks before it arrives — the children hear the songs and feel spring coming. Classic spring songs: In the Springtime Little Bunnies Go Hop Hop (circle movement song) · The Farmer is Working the Fields (farming rhythm song, Grade 3) · Humble Bumble Bees Are Buzzing (nature song, variable tempo) · Down by the Station · Spring nature rounds. Seeds, blossoms, bees, birds returning.
March–May
☀️ Summer / St. John's Songs
Midsummer songs celebrating the sun at its height. Fire songs, songs of warmth and light, outdoor singing. The Sun with Loving Light is especially powerful at Midsummer. Outdoor circle games and singing games are at their richest in June. Water songs for water play.
June · St. John's Day
🍁 Autumn Songs
Autumn Leaves Are Falling Down · Put On Your Dresses of Red and Gold · Autumn Good Morning, Summer Good Night · harvest songs, apple picking songs, hedgehog and squirrel preparing for winter. Michaelmas dragon songs for older children. Warm, earthy tones. Songs slow down as the year breathes in.
September–November
🕯️ Martinmas Songs — November
Lantern songs are among the most beautiful in the Waldorf tradition. Children make paper lanterns and walk in procession after dark. I Go With My Little Lantern (German: Laterne Laterne) is sung in schools across Europe, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Also: St. Martin sharing his cloak song.
November 11
🌟 Advent Songs
The Advent garden is accompanied by the most beloved songs of the Waldorf year. Flicker Little Candle · Sunlight Fast is Dwindling · Glimmer Lantern Glimmer · The Earth Was Dark. Songs grow quieter and more inward through the four weeks of Advent, building to the profound stillness of Christmas. The Advent spiral walk is done in silence, broken only by song.
December · Advent
❄️ Winter Songs
Snow songs, frost songs, songs of the sleeping earth. Where Are the Froggies When the North Wind Blows? · star songs, animal sleep songs, cozy warmth and hearth songs. The mood is inward, hushed, tender. Winter songs are the most lullaby-like of the year.
December–February
🌼 Easter / Spring Festival Songs
Resurrection songs, butterfly songs, seed-growing songs. Blessings on the Blossoms · Down by the Station Rainbow Fairies. Easter songs celebrate transformation — the caterpillar becoming a butterfly, the seed becoming a plant — with great joy and light.
March–April · Easter
🐉 Michaelmas Songs — September
Songs of courage, light overcoming darkness, the archangel Michael and the dragon. Michael and the Dragon songs for Grades 3–5. Rowan berry songs, iron songs, harvest songs. Michaelmas songs have a different quality — stronger, more martial, calling the child to courage as the darker half of the year approaches.
September 29 · Michaelmas

🇪🇸🇦🇷🇲🇽 Canciones de Ronda & Corro — Waldorf en Español
Más de 120 canciones pentatónicas, rondas y juegos de dedos usados en jardines Waldorf en español — ordenados por estación, momento del día y festividad. Las canciones de ronda en los jardines Waldorf son pentatónicas. Rudolf Steiner recomendó la escala pentatónica especialmente para el primer septenio (0–7 años), ya que ofrece al niño un espacio sonoro abierto y libre. La ronda une canto, movimiento y ritmo en una misma experiencia artística.

🌙 Calendar of the Soul — Rudolf Steiner's 52 Weekly Verses Free daily resource · Current verse · All 52 verses · Northern & Southern Hemisphere ▾
What is the Calendar of the Soul? "The course of the year has its own life. The human soul can sympathise with this life." — Rudolf Steiner, 1918.

The Calendar of the Soul (Anthroposophischer Seelenkalender) was first created by Rudolf Steiner in 1912 — the same year as the founding of the Anthroposophical Society. It consists of 52 weekly verses, one for each week of the year, beginning at Easter and moving through the full seasonal cycle. Each verse captures the specific quality of that week's relationship between the human soul and the cosmos — the breathing-out of the earth from spring to summer, and the breathing-in from autumn to winter's depths.

Rudolf Steiner writes: "The course of the year has its own life. The human soul can sympathise with this life. If it allows what speaks differently from week to week from the life of the year to have an effect on it, then it will only find itself properly through such co-existence. She will feel how this gives her strength from within."

These are not poems to be read — they are meditations to be lived. Read the verse slowly, once in the morning and once in the evening, for the full seven days. Let it resonate rather than be understood. Steiner said: "These formulae for meditation do in all reality lead the soul out of its narrow confines to experience of the heavens. I can assure you that the results of long, long occult investigations are contained in these 52 verses."
🌿 This Week's Verse — Live
Loading this week's verse…

The verse updates automatically each week. Begins at Easter each year. rsarchive.org/COTS — find the full calendar with all translators.

✨ How to Work with the Calendar of the Soul
Read slowly, twice daily
Read the verse once in the morning on waking, and once in the evening before sleep. Do not try to analyse or understand it intellectually. Let the images and language wash over you. The meaning will deepen through the week.
Memorise it
By midweek, try to recall the verse from memory. Saying it quietly to yourself while walking, doing housework or tending the garden brings it deeper into your life. The verse becomes a companion — always available in the inner world.
Connect it to what you see
The verses are mirrors of the outer world. In late summer you feel the light drawing inward; in deep winter a warmth stirs from within. Notice how the verse speaks to what you observe in nature that week — the length of day, the quality of light, the temperature of the air.
The counter verse
Steiner marked each verse from Spring-Summer-Autumn (1–26) with a letter of the alphabet and matched them with corresponding verses for Autumn-Winter-Spring (27–52). This pairing reveals a magnificent polarity of opposing forces that influence the soul striving through the seasons, travelling the path of a lemniscate. The verse exactly opposite yours in the year is your "counter verse" — read both together for depth.
Northern vs Southern Hemisphere
The first verse starts with Easter during the blossoming of Spring in the Northern Hemisphere. Since it is autumn in the Southern Hemisphere, Week 27 may be a more appropriate starting point on Easter Sunday for those in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, South America. The southern verses begin at the autumn/winter quality and mirror north.
Share it with children
The verses are deep for young children as written — but their essence can be distilled into a morning verse or nature observation for the family. "This week our verse speaks of the light drawing inward — let's notice together how the days are growing shorter." The Calendar connects home and cosmos.
🌍 The Structure of the Year — Soul Breathing
SeasonVersesSoul MoodCosmic Quality
🌱 Spring · EasterWeeks 1–7The soul breathes out with the earth. Thoughts dissolve into the light. The self expands into the world.The earth breathes out — forces stream upward. "The world-enveloping spirit pours its light into my soul."
☀️ Early SummerWeeks 8–13Maximum outpouring. The soul is most fully merged with the world. The self is least conscious of itself.Midsummer — the earth is most outbreathed. The sun at its height. St. John's fires. Pure light.
🌞 High Summer · MidsummerWeeks 14–20The first whisper of return. The light begins to draw inward. A seed of self-awareness quickens.After the summer solstice, the days begin to shorten. The first turn inward.
🍂 Michaelmas · AutumnWeeks 21–26 / 27The soul turns inward. The self awakens. The earth breathes in. Courage is called for.Michaelmas (Week 26) — the midpoint. The equal crossing of the lemniscate. The soul must find its own light.
🍁 Late AutumnWeeks 28–34The soul finds its own warmth. Inner light must replace outer light. Self-reliance deepens.The earth breathes inward. Forces draw into root and seed. The stars speak more clearly.
❄️ Advent · WinterWeeks 35–43Maximum inwardness. The soul's own light is most needed. The Christ impulse stirs in the darkness.The winter solstice. The earth most fully inbreathed. Seeds wait in darkness. The turning point.
🌟 Winter into SpringWeeks 44–52The soul holds its inner light as the outer light returns. Balancing inner gain against outer expansion.The light returns. The forces begin to stir upward again toward Easter and the new cycle.
